body_markdown:
The quarterly update of the Hagerty Price Guide went live at the beginning of October, and as usual we’ve highlighted the[ups](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/hagerty-price-guide/5-cars-gaining-value-in-a-split-market/) and[downs](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/5-vehicles-shedding-value-in-a-lopsided-market/) over the previous three months. We also like to zero in on certain segments, because the[30,000-foot view](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-indexes-underscore-a-mixed-market/) of the collector car market never quite tells the whole story.


This week, we’ll take a look at one of the biggest segments of all—American muscle cars—to see what’s up and what’s down this quarter. Although Hagerty’s American Muscle Car Index was flat for October, there was still a decent amount of movement for some individual cars. The biggest ones are below, measured by the average increase or decrease in condition #2 (excellent) value.


*Have questions about how we arrived at these changes? You can read more about the methodology behind the Hagerty Price Guide[here](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/how-the-hagerty-price-guide-is-made/) .*


## 1968–70 Dodge Charger (Hemi)


Mecum


**Average increase: +15%**


Dodge gave the Charger a crisp redesign for[1968](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1968+Dodge+Charger) , and it was a hit, truly one of the most elegant takes on the wasp-waisted, Coke-bottle shape popularized in the muscle car’s golden age. Most famous as the bad-guy car in *Bullitt* and the good-guy car in *The Dukes of Hazzard* , the second-gen Charger was only available in one body style, but it could be had in base, R/T, and 500 trims.


It could also be had with several V-8s, including the 318, 383, 440, and 426. This past quarter, though, the answer to “[That thang got a Hemi?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-gV7fXH45FA) ” really had to be “yes,” as far as the market was concerned. Values for most versions of the second-gen Charger have been flat or close to it for the past several years, and a handful of them are down with the latest update, but the[426-cubic-inch, 425-horsepower Hemi](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/dodge/charger/1970/1970-dodge-charger-r!!t?id=aCn1I000000CxEsSAK) premium just got much bigger with that engine’s 15% increase, following some huge sales over the summer. Condition #2 values now range from $160,000 to $189,000, while the rest of the 1968–72 Charger lineup mostly sits in the mid-five-figure range.


## 1968–72 Buick GS 400 and GS 455


Hagerty Marketplace | Matt_Lowney


**Average increase: +4%**


Buick’s lesser-known answer to the[Pontiac GTO](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1964+pontiac+gto) , the Gran Sport (shortened to GS in 1967, and spelled out again in ’73) first arrived in 1965 and was based on the[Skylark](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1965+buick+skylark) . Built through 1972, it was Buick’s last truly sporty offering, until the Grand National arrived 10 years later.


Muscle car buyers were spoiled for choice in the late ’60s/early ’70s, even just in the Buick lineup. The ’68 GS started with a 350-cu-in/280-hp V-8 but got more potent with the GS 400’s 400-cu-in/340-hp unit. A Stage 1 package introduced in 1969 added more performance upgrades, while 1970 brought an available 455-cu-in V-8 and the flashy, fully loaded[GSX](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=buick+gsx) .


Today, GSXs can command six figures in excellent condition. Regular GSs come at a much more modest price, but after several quarters of decreases, most 400- and 455-powered cars rebounded with a small but significant increase in October. Condition #2 values currently range from $27,700 for a[’72 GS 455 Sport Coupe](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/buick/gs/1972/1972-buick-gs-455?id=aCn1I000000DIT8SAO) all the way up to $129K for a[’70 GS 455 Stage I convertible](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/buick/gs/1970/1970-buick-gs-455_stage_i?id=aCn1I000000Cx2XSAS) .


## 2005–14 Ford Mustang GT


Mecum


**Average increase: +7%**


With the fifth-gen Mustang, aka the S197, Ford arguably did retro styling better than anybody else in the 2000s. This was also the last live-axle Mustang, and the first to get the Coyote V-8 (in 2011). Bullitts, California Specials, and several different Shelby models spiced up the S197 platform, but the most popular way to get into rear-drive V-8 fun was, as always, ticking the box for a regular ol’[Mustang GT](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ford/mustang/2007/2007-ford-mustang-shelby_gt?id=aCn1I000000CvIuSAK) .


Despite not being that old, and despite there being newer, quicker, and readily available V-8 Mustangs out there, S197 GTs have increased in value every quarter this year. And even though they’re up 34% compared to January, they’re still one of the more affordable ways to hoon a car made in this century. Condition #2 values range from the mid-20s to high-30s, while condition #3 (good) values range from the mid-teens to mid-20s.


## 1965–68 Ford Mustang GT


Mecum


**Average decrease: -4%**


Even though newer Mustangs are gaining ground, some older ones are softening. The first-gen pony cars, particularly the original 1965–68 versions, are among the most popular classic cars in this country, whether you measure by sales volume, insurance quote activity, or really anything else. They’re also quite varied in terms of equipment, options, and body styles.


As a result, the market for early Mustangs is quite nuanced, and there’s variety even among just the[GT models](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1966+ford+mustang+gt) . Most of them depreciated this past quarter, however, with drops ranging from 2% to 8%, and current #2 values range from $20,300 to well into six figures. It’s a bit surprising to see a stalwart of the hobby get less expensive when so much else is getting pricier, but first-gen Mustangs are popular enough and have a broad enough demographic appeal that this correction isn’t likely to be a severe long-term trend.


## 1968–71 Pontiac GTO


Mecum


**Average decrease: -3%**


The genre-defining GTO got its first major redesign for 1968, and *Motor Trend* voted it “Car of the Year.” Typical of the era, buyers had a headache-inducing amount of choice on the order sheet, with a variety of 400- and 455-cu-in engines; Ram Air I, II, III, and IV packages; Hardtop coupes and convertibles; Judge trims; and all sorts of tasty paint colors. In some years there were more than 20 shades to choose from.


Like the first-gen Mustang, the second-gen GTO is a quintessential piece of classic muscle that took a somewhat surprising step back this past quarter. Unlike the everlasting Mustang, though, there is no longer a GTO to connect to today. There isn’t even a Pontiac. And as the brand fades further into the mists of history, we’ll see how much staying power the Goat really has. Decreases for the 1968–71 cars were 4% nearly across the board (except for the Ram Air IV), and #2 values currently run from the $40K range for lower-output coupes to six figures for certain soft-top Judges. The one exception here is GTOs equipped with the rare and potent Ram Air IV engine. These cars exist in a much higher price bracket, and without any reliable sales data this past period, their values stayed flat.


## 1970 Plymouth Road Runner Superbird


Hagerty Marketplace


**Average decrease: -9%**


Based on the[Road Runner](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/search?q=1970+plymouth+road+runner) and decorated with the famous Looney Tunes character on its ridiculous rear wing, the 1970-only Plymouth Superbird also had Looney Tunes proportions. Not to look good, but to go faster on the NASCAR ovals. And go faster it did, with drivers Richard Petty and Pete Hamilton both racking up wins throughout the Superbird’s one and only season in the sport. Plymouth also offered a road-going Superbird for speed freaks, powered by either a 440-cu-in/370-hp four-barrel, 440-cu-in/390-hp 3×2 Six Pack, or 426-cu-in/425-hp Hemi. The car’s massive beak and high wing weren’t exactly practical on the street, and about 2000 Superbirds were built in total.


Superbird values have flown up and down over the past few years, and they still haven’t found a steady altitude, though they are fairly expensive. Condition #2 values are down the least for the Hemi-powered cars at a 4% drop (to $384K), while the 440-cu-in/390-hp cars are down 9% (to $265K) and the 440-cu-in/375-hp cars 14% (to $154K).
